summary.heading: 6. A friendly who’s-who: the thinkers behind the five proofs, and the critics who keep coming back
summary.plain: Feser’s five arguments are named after five thinkers: Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, and Leibniz. You do not need to have read any of them. You just need to know roughly who they were and what idea each one is famous for, so that the chapter titles stop being intimidating. The same is true for the critics — Hume, Kant, Russell, and today’s New Atheists — whose objections come up again and again.
summary.body:
Feser is careful in his Introduction to say that he is not writing commentary on anyone. He defends *an* Aristotelian proof, not Aristotle’s own proof; *an* Augustinian proof, not an interpretation of anything Augustine actually wrote. The names mark a family resemblance, not a homework assignment. Here is the cast.

**Plato (c. 428–348 B.C.)** taught that the general patterns we find in the world — triangularity, justice, redness — are more real than the individual things that copy them. He placed these **Forms** in a realm of their own, independent of minds and of physical things. Chapter 3 uses Plato’s insight but rejects his separate realm.

**Aristotle (384–322 B.C.)** was Plato’s student and the origin of most of the book’s vocabulary. He analyzed change as the **actualization of a potential**, distinguished **substance** from **accident**, **form** from **matter**, and named **four causes**. His argument from change to an **Unmoved Mover** is the ancestor of chapter 1.

**Plotinus (c. 204–270)** founded what we now call Neo-Platonism. He argued that everything composite depends on what is utterly non-composite, which he called **the One**. Chapter 2 is the modern descendant of that argument.

**Augustine (354–430)** took Plato’s Forms and relocated them: they are not free-floating in a third realm but are ideas in the mind of God. Chapter 3 develops that move rigorously.

**Aquinas (1225–1274)**, the greatest of the **Scholastics** (the medieval university philosophers and theologians), synthesized Aristotle with Christian theology. He is famous for the **Five Ways**, but Feser explicitly says this book is *not* about them. Chapter 4 uses a different argument of his, from his early work on being and essence: the **real distinction** between essence and existence.

**Leibniz (1646–1716)** was a mathematician and philosopher who made the **principle of sufficient reason** central. Chapter 5 defends a version of his argument, though Feser interprets it in an Aristotelian-Thomistic rather than a continental-rationalist way.

Now the critics. **David Hume (1711–1776)** attacked the idea that we can know necessary causal connections and is the source of the objection that a series of explained items needs no further explanation. **Immanuel Kant (1724–1804)** argued that metaphysics oversteps the limits of human reason and that all cosmological arguments secretly depend on the **ontological argument**. **Bertrand Russell (1872–1970)** popularized the reply that the universe might be “just there,” a **brute fact**. The **New Atheists** — Richard Dawkins, Christopher Hitchens, Sam Harris, Daniel Dennett, Lawrence Krauss, A. C. Grayling, Alex Rosenberg and others — are the recent popular critics. Feser treats their standard objections in chapter 7 and judges them, bluntly, to be much weaker than their reputation.
summary.takeaway: The five proofs are named for five thinkers whose core insights they develop — Aristotle on change, Plotinus on parts, Augustine on universals, Aquinas on essence and existence, Leibniz on explanation — and the recurring critics are Hume, Kant, Russell, and the New Atheists.
summary.deepDive:
**Why the labels are not exegesis.** In his Introduction Feser is unusually explicit about this: the arguments are inspired by these thinkers and, he believes, capture what is essential to them, but he is not claiming any of them would have endorsed everything he says. This matters practically. If a critic says “but Aristotle thought the heavenly spheres rotated eternally, and that’s false,” he has missed the point. Feser’s view is that the outdated science is a husk around a philosophical kernel that does not depend on it. You will see the same move in chapter 1 when he insists that the argument survives Newton, Einstein, and quantum mechanics.

**A useful mental filing system.** Try associating each thinker with one question:

- Aristotle: *how is change even possible?*
- Plotinus: *what holds a thing’s parts together?*
- Augustine: *where do the general patterns live?*
- Aquinas: *why does a thing exist at all, given that what it is doesn’t include that it is?*
- Leibniz: *why is there anything rather than nothing?*

Each of the five proofs is the long answer to one of those five questions. If you can recall the question, you can usually reconstruct the shape of the argument.

**On the word “Scholastic.”** Scholasticism was the philosophy of the medieval schools — the universities of Paris, Oxford, Bologna. Its hallmarks are precise distinctions, technical Latin vocabulary, and the method of stating objections before replying. When Feser uses phrases like *per se*, *per accidens*, *agere sequitur esse*, or *ex nihilo nihil fit*, he is speaking Scholastic. He also draws on later **Neo-Scholastic** manual writers such as Garrigou-Lagrange, whose formulations of the principle of sufficient reason he quotes in chapter 5.

**The usual confusion.** Beginners often assume the book is a history of philosophy, and read anxiously, worried they should already know these figures. It is not. It is a work of philosophy that uses history for orientation. Meeting a name you do not recognize is never a reason to stop reading; Feser almost always explains the relevant idea on the spot.

**How it feeds the arguments.** The one historical point that does real work is the contrast between Plato’s third realm and Augustine’s divine ideas in chapter 3. There, rejecting Plato’s version is a step in the argument, not just background colour.

checks.q: Feser says his book is NOT…
options: a defense of arguments for God’s existence
a book about Aquinas’ Five Ways
aimed at non-specialist readers
concerned with God’s attributes
checks.explanation: The Introduction opens by saying this is not a book about the Five Ways. It is a defense of five arguments, two of which are in Aquinas and three of which are not; it does address God’s attributes and is aimed at non-specialists.

checks.q: Which thinker is associated with the claim that everything composite depends on something absolutely non-composite?
options: Plotinus
Hume
Leibniz
Kant
checks.explanation: Plotinus called the absolutely simple source “the One.” The Neo-Platonic proof of chapter 2 develops this. Leibniz is associated with the principle of sufficient reason; Hume and Kant are critics.

checks.q: A friend says: “Aristotle believed in crystal spheres carrying the planets, so the Aristotelian proof is obsolete.” The best reply is…
options: Aristotle never held any scientific views
modern astronomy actually supports crystal spheres
the argument’s core does not depend on that outdated astronomy; Feser restates it without it
we should accept Aristotle’s science on his authority
checks.explanation: Feser says the essential kernel of the argument does not depend on the archaic scientific husk in which earlier writers expressed it. Chapter 1 presents the argument as it would be made today.

summary.heading: 7. Aristotle’s toolkit: substance and accident, form and matter, the four causes, actuality and potentiality
summary.plain: Aristotle noticed some very ordinary things and gave them names. A thing (a dog) is different from its features (its brown colour). A thing’s shape or organization is different from the stuff it is made of. There are four different things we can mean when we ask “why?” And a thing can be a certain way already, or merely be able to become that way. Those four pairs are the whole toolkit, and every one of them comes from noticing something you already knew.
summary.body:
**Substance and accident.** A **substance** is a thing that exists in its own right: this dog, this oak tree, this person, this stone. An **accident** is a feature that exists only *in* a substance: the dog’s brown colour, its weight of forty pounds, its current position on the rug. Brownness does not go for a walk by itself. Notice this is not the everyday sense of “accident” (a mishap); it comes from Latin *accidens*, “what happens to” something. Feser also distinguishes, in chapter 6, between accidents that merely happen to a thing (a person’s skin colour) and **properties** in the strict sense — features that flow from what the thing is, like a human being’s capacity to find things funny.

**Form and matter.** Every physical thing is a combination of **matter** — the stuff — and **form** — the organization or pattern that makes the stuff be that kind of thing. A marble statue and a marble slab have similar matter and different forms. A **substantial form** makes a thing the kind of thing it is (what makes this matter be a dog rather than a heap); an **accidental form** merely modifies an already-existing thing (its being brown). This pair, called **hylomorphism** (from Greek *hylē*, matter, and *morphē*, form), matters in chapter 2, where form and matter count as metaphysical parts, and in chapter 6, where Feser explains that a thing’s activities follow from its form — the principle *agere sequitur esse*, “action follows being.”

**The four causes.** For Aristotle, to ask why something is the way it is can mean four different questions. Take a wooden chair.

1. **Material cause**: what it is made of — wood.
2. **Formal cause**: what it is, its pattern or structure — the chair-shape and organization.
3. **Efficient cause**: what brought it about — the carpenter.
4. **Final cause**: what it is for, what it naturally tends toward — being sat on.

Modern people usually mean only the efficient cause by “cause,” which is a large part of why classical arguments get misread. Feser uses the efficient sense most, but the principle of proportionate causality trades on formal causality too.

**Actuality and potentiality.** This is the key pair. **Actuality** (Latin *actus*) is the way a thing is right now: the coffee is actually hot, actually liquid, actually in a cup. **Potentiality** (Latin *potentia*) is a real capacity a thing has but is not exercising: the coffee is potentially cold, potentially spilled, potentially a stain on the carpet. Crucially, potentials are limited by what the thing is: the coffee can become cold, but it has no potential to become chicken soup or to turn into a live chicken. So potentiality is not the same as nothing — it is a real feature of a real thing, halfway (as it were) between actual existence and sheer nonexistence. That is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides, who argued that change is impossible because it would require something to come from nothing. Change is not something from nothing; it is the **actualization of a potential**.
summary.takeaway: A substance is a thing, an accident is a feature of a thing; form is a thing’s organizing pattern and matter its stuff; “cause” can mean material, formal, efficient, or final; and every changeable thing is a mixture of what it actually is and what it merely could be.
summary.deepDive:
**Why potentiality is not a dodge.** Newcomers often suspect that “potentiality” is a word that explains nothing — a bit of medieval hand-waving, like saying opium causes sleep because it has a dormitive power. Feser meets this head-on in chapter 6 when John Cottingham complains that potentiality makes the principle of proportionate causality trivially true. The reply is that potentials are *discriminating*. Say that the coffee has a potential to become cold and you have said something false of a stone statue that is already at room temperature and something false of the number seven. Say the coffee has a potential to become chicken soup and you have said something false. A concept that rules things out is not empty. Explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, Feser grants, but minimally informative is not uninformative.

**A worked example.** Put a glass of water in the freezer. Before freezing, the water is *actually* liquid and *potentially* solid. It is not potentially a violin. When the freezer removes heat, something already actual (the cold coil, the surrounding air) reduces the water’s potential-to-be-solid to actuality. Now run the four causes on the ice cube: material cause, H₂O; formal cause, the crystalline structure that makes it ice rather than steam; efficient cause, the freezer; final cause, in Aristotle’s sense, the natural tendency of water at that temperature to form that structure. All four are answers to “why?” and none competes with the others.

**The qualification that trips people up.** Feser is careful in chapter 1 to say he did *not* claim that whatever causes a change must itself be changing. That does not follow, and he thinks it is false. The claim is conditional: *if* the changer is itself being changed, *then* that change needs a changer too. Missing that qualification produces the bad objection “so God must be changing too.” Nothing in the argument requires it; step 4 of the formal argument says only that a potential cannot actualize itself.

**How it feeds the argument.** Steps 1–5 of chapter 1’s fifty-step argument are just this toolkit made explicit: change is real; change is the actualization of a potential; therefore actualization of potentials is real; nothing actualizes a potential except something already actual; therefore every change is caused by something already actual. Every later step rests on those five.

**The usual confusion.** People hear “potential” and think of statistics or capability in a loose sense (“she has potential”). Aristotle’s sense is metaphysical: a real, specific, presently-unrealized capacity grounded in what a thing actually is.

checks.q: In Aristotle’s sense, which of these is an accident rather than a substance?
options: this oak tree
this dog
the dog’s brown colour
this human being
checks.explanation: A substance exists in its own right; an accident exists only in a substance. Brownness does not exist on its own — it exists in the dog.

checks.q: “The chair is for sitting on.” Which of the four causes is this?
options: final cause
material cause
efficient cause
formal cause
checks.explanation: The final cause is what a thing is for or tends toward. The material cause would be the wood, the efficient cause the carpenter, the formal cause the chair-structure.

checks.q: Why does Feser say a potential is not the same as nothing?
options: because potentials can be measured scientifically
because everything is potentially everything else
because potentials only exist in the mind
because a thing has some potentials and lacks others — coffee can grow cold but cannot become chicken soup
checks.explanation: The fact that a thing has specific potentials and not others shows that potentiality is a real feature of the thing, which is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides’ claim that change would require something coming from nothing.

summary.heading: 8. Causation as Feser means it: actualizing a potential, here-and-now causes, and the two kinds of causal series
summary.plain: This is the most important lesson in the whole module, so take it slowly. When Feser asks what causes something, he usually is not asking what got it started in the past. He is asking what is holding it in being right now. And he says there are two very different kinds of causal chain: one strung out over time, like a line of ancestors, and one stacked up at this moment, like a cup on a desk on a floor. Only the second kind needs a first member — and “first” there does not mean “earliest.”
summary.body:
Start with the definition. For Feser, a **cause** in the central sense is whatever **actualizes a potential**. The cool air actualizes the coffee’s potential to be cold. The desk actualizes the cup’s potential to be three feet off the ground. Notice that the second example involves no change over time at all — nothing is happening to the cup — yet a potential is being actualized continuously.

That leads to the crucial shift of question. Ask “what caused this cup of coffee?” and you will naturally answer: someone poured hot water through grounds twenty minutes ago. That is a **cause in the past**, and it is not what the arguments are about. Feser asks a different question: what makes it true that the coffee exists *right now*, at this instant? Not how it got here, and not what might destroy it later, but what sustains it in being at each moment it exists. The water exists only because certain potentials of hydrogen and oxygen atoms are actualized as water rather than as separate gases; the atoms exist only because certain potentials of subatomic particles are being actualized in this arrangement rather than another. That is a **here-and-now** or **sustaining** cause.

Now the distinction everything turns on.

A **linear series** (traditionally called a series ordered **per accidens**, “accidentally”) runs backwards through time, and each member keeps its causal power once it has it. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you. Your grandfather can be dead and your father can still father children. You pressed a button, the air conditioner came on; you can leave the house and it goes on cooling. The members have their own power.

A **hierarchical series** (traditionally **per se**, “essentially”) is different. The coffee cup is three feet above the floor because the desk holds it up; the desk stays up because the floor holds it; the floor because the foundation; the foundation because the earth. Here, every member other than the first has its power only **derivatively** — it is borrowing. The desk does not have, on its own, any power to keep a cup aloft. Remove the floor and the desk and cup go down together. Feser’s image is that the intermediate members are like **instruments**: a brush does not paint a picture, the painter paints with the brush.

And that is why a hierarchical series must have a first member while a linear one need not. **“First” here does not mean earliest in time.** It means non-derivative: something with the power built in, which can actualize without having to be actualized. Feser makes the point unforgettable with the infinite paintbrush: a brush cannot move itself, and it would still not be able to move itself if its handle were infinitely long. Length does not manufacture power. An infinite stack of desks would hold up a cup exactly as well as one desk does — that is, not at all.

This is why the famous objections misfire. “Maybe the universe is infinitely old” is irrelevant, because the arguments concede that for the sake of argument and then ask about the here-and-now series instead. “Why can’t the regress be infinite?” has an answer for hierarchical series specifically: an infinite series of borrowers never produces a lender. And “Who made God?” asks what actualized the potentials in something that, by the argument’s conclusion, has no potentials to actualize.
summary.takeaway: A cause, for Feser, is what actualizes a potential here and now; a linear (per accidens) series running back through time may in principle be infinite, but a hierarchical (per se) series of borrowed power must terminate in something with non-derivative power — and “first” means non-derivative, not earliest.
summary.deepDive:
**Simultaneity is a teaching aid, not the definition.** Feser is explicit and careful about this, and it is worth getting right. He introduces hierarchical series with simultaneous examples (cup, desk, floor; lamp, chain, fixture, ceiling) because they are easy to picture. But what *makes* a series hierarchical is not that its members exist at the same moment. It is the **derivative or instrumental character** of the later members: they have their causal power only insofar as they are receiving it from something else at the moment they exercise it. A critic who says “but relativity shows simultaneity is frame-relative” has therefore attacked the scaffolding rather than the building. Chapter 1 makes exactly this reply.

**A thought experiment to run yourself.** Put a book on a shelf. Ask: why is the book not on the floor? Because the shelf. Why is the shelf not on the floor? Because its brackets. Why the brackets? The wall. The wall? The foundation. The earth. Now notice two things. First, each answer is about *this instant*, not history. Second, if at any point you found a member with no support and no power of its own — a shelf that just hovers as an unexplained brute fact — the whole chain of “explanations” would be exposed as fake, because a thing with no tendency to stay aloft cannot impart such a tendency to the book. That is precisely the argument Feser uses in chapter 5 against brute facts as terminators of explanation, and it is the same structural point as here.

**Why the earth is not really first.** Feser flags in chapter 1 that even the earth is not a first cause in the strict sense, and returns to it. The earth holds things up only because it exists, and its existing is itself the actualization of potentials of its parts. Once you start asking not “what holds it up?” but “what holds it *in being*?”, you get a new hierarchical series whose members are far more fundamental than desks and floors, and that is the series the proof actually rides on. The staircase example is a ladder you kick away.

**How it feeds the formal argument.** This is what secures steps 7–13 of chapter 1’s fifty-step argument: the existence of a substance at any moment presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence (7–8); its actualizer either is purely actual or is itself being actualized (9); the second option generates a regress that is hierarchical (10–11); hierarchical regresses cannot be infinite (11); so there is a purely actual actualizer (12–14).

**The usual confusion.** People hear “first cause” and picture a starting gun at the Big Bang. Every time you catch yourself picturing a timeline, stop and picture a stack instead.

checks.q: Which is a hierarchical (per se) series?
options: a chandelier held by a chain held by a ceiling fixture
a father who begot a son who begot a grandson
one domino knocking over the next in a long row
a series of past kings, each succeeding the last
checks.explanation: In the chandelier case each member holds only because it is simultaneously being held; its power is derivative. The other three are linear series whose members retain power independently once they have acted.

checks.q: In this context, calling a cause “first” means that it…
options: existed before anything else in time
occurred at the Big Bang
is the most powerful member of the series
has its causal power built in rather than derived from anything else
checks.explanation: Feser stresses that “first” here is not temporal. A first cause is one with non-derivative, non-instrumental causal power. That is why an infinitely long brush handle would still need a painter.

checks.q: A skeptic says: “Cosmology may show the universe is infinitely old, which sinks this argument.” The best reply is:
options: cosmology has proven the universe had a beginning
the argument grants an infinitely old universe for the sake of argument and asks instead what sustains things in being at each moment
philosophy is unaffected by any scientific result
an infinitely old universe would itself be a hierarchical series
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for the sake of argument. His argument concerns hierarchical, here-and-now series, so the age of the universe is beside the point.

summary.heading: 9. Essence and existence — and what philosophers mean by a “real distinction”
summary.plain: There are two different things you can know about a lion: what a lion is, and whether there are any. Knowing the first does not tell you the second — which is a clue that these are two genuinely different features of reality, not just two ways of talking. Feser calls that a real distinction, and chapter 4 is built on it.
summary.body:
Take any ordinary thing — a stone, a tree, a dog, a person. Two quite different things can be known about it. First, **what it is**: its nature, definition, kind. Philosophers call this its **essence**. Second, **that it is**: the fact that it is actually out there in reality and not merely a concept. Philosophers call this its **existence**.

Now, some distinctions are merely verbal. “Bachelor” and “unmarried man” pick out exactly the same thing; the difference is in our words, not in the world. Philosophers call that a **distinction of reason**. Others reflect something in things themselves as they are apart from our thinking, and those are called **real distinctions**. Chapter 4 argues that the distinction between essence and existence in ordinary things is a real one, and gives three reasons.

**First, from knowledge.** Describe lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns to someone who has never heard of any of them, telling him exactly what each is. Then ask which exists, which used to exist, and which never existed. He cannot tell, however complete his grasp of their natures. But what a thing is belongs to its objective reality, and if a thing exists, so does the fact that it exists. So if essence and existence were not distinct features of reality, grasping the first would deliver the second. It does not.

**Second, from contingency.** Lions exist, but if the history of life had gone differently they would not have, and they might one day be extinct. If a lion’s existence were not really distinct from its essence, it would have existence simply by being what it is — it would exist by its very nature, and so could not possibly fail to exist. It would be **necessary**, not contingent. Since it is contingent, the distinction is real.

**Third, from uniqueness.** Suppose something in which essence and existence are *not* distinct — something whose essence just *is* existence. Feser argues there could be at most one such thing. To have two, you would need something to differentiate them, and any differentiating feature would make each of them “existence itself PLUS something,” and so not existence itself after all. But stones, trees, dogs and human beings come in multiples. Therefore in each of them essence and existence must be distinct.

Put those together and the chapter’s engine starts: anything in which essence and existence are really distinct needs something to conjoin them at every moment it exists, which is a hierarchical dependence, which must terminate in something whose essence just is existence — what the tradition calls **subsistent existence itself**, *ipsum esse subsistens*.

One warning about vocabulary. **Essence** is not a vague word for “the gist” or “the important part.” It means the nature that makes a thing the kind of thing it is. And **existence** here is not a property in a list of properties; it is the fact that the essence is actually instantiated out there at all.
summary.takeaway: In every ordinary thing, what it is and the fact that it is are two genuinely different features of reality — a real distinction, not merely a distinction in our way of speaking — and that is what makes such things need a cause of their existence at every moment.
summary.deepDive:
**Real distinction versus distinction of reason, carefully.** This is a beginner’s stumbling block, so make it concrete. “The Morning Star” and “The Evening Star” both pick out Venus: distinction of reason, because reality contains one object. “The cup” and “the desk” pick out two things: a real distinction of things. Essence and existence are trickier, because essence and existence are not two *things* sitting side by side. The claim is that within one thing there are two really different metaphysical aspects or **principles** — not two objects, but not merely two descriptions either. Chapter 2 will treat them as *metaphysical parts*, which is exactly why the Neo-Platonic and Thomistic proofs turn out to be relatives.

**The objection Feser anticipates.** Someone will say: the first argument assumes we grasp essences completely, which we usually do not; maybe existence is hiding inside the essence where we cannot see it. Feser’s reply turns on a nice distinction between **incompletely conceiving** and **misconceiving**. If you know a lion is an animal but do not know it is a cat, your grasp is incomplete but not mistaken. If you judge that a lion is *not* a cat, you have misconceived it. Now: if you judge that lions do not exist — say you think they are extinct, or fictional — you have judged falsely, but you have not misconceived what a lion is. Yet if existence were part of the essence, denying existence would be as much a misconception as denying felinity. It is not. So existence is not part of the essence.

**A second objection, and its answer.** Why not say a lion is contingent simply because it has causes and can be killed? Because that gets things backwards. The question is why a thing would need a cause of its existence in the first place, or could have a potential for non-existence at all, if existence were already included in what it is. Appealing to causes and vulnerabilities presupposes the real distinction rather than replacing it.

**How it feeds the argument.** In the worked simplified argument later in this module, the premise that a thing’s existing here and now is the actualization of its potential for existence is the Aristotelian way of saying what chapter 4 says in the language of essence and existence. The two chapters are the same insight in two dialects.

**The usual confusion.** People suspect a word trick — “you have just defined God into existence.” Not so: the argument does not start from a definition of God but from an observed feature of ordinary lions and stones, and reaches its conclusion by asking what could possibly account for that feature.

checks.q: A distinction of reason is one that…
options: can only be drawn by trained philosophers
reflects our way of thinking or speaking rather than a difference in the thing itself
reflects a genuine difference in reality apart from our minds
is always mistaken
checks.explanation: “Bachelor” and “unmarried man” differ only in our way of speaking. A real distinction, by contrast, tracks something in mind-independent reality.

checks.q: The argument from contingency for the real distinction says that if a lion’s existence were identical to its essence, then…
options: lions would be unknowable
lions would exist by their very nature and so could not fail to exist
lions would have no causes
there could be no more than one lion
checks.explanation: If existence were included in what a lion is, a lion would exist necessarily. Since lions are contingent — they might never have existed and might go extinct — essence and existence must be really distinct in them.

checks.q: You fully describe unicorns, lions, and pterodactyls to someone unfamiliar with all three, then ask which exists. He cannot say. What does Feser conclude?
options: that essences are unknowable
that existence is a mere linguistic convention
that his description of the essences must have been incomplete
that a thing’s existence is really distinct from its essence, since grasping the one does not deliver the other
checks.explanation: Both essence and existence are part of a thing’s objective reality. If they were not distinct, knowing the essence would settle the existence. It does not — hence the real distinction.

summary.heading: 10. The principle of sufficient reason and the principle of causality, in plain words
summary.plain: Two principles do a lot of work in this book, and they are not the same. One says that nothing goes from being merely possible to being actual all by itself. The other says that everything has an explanation of some kind. Neither says “everything has a cause,” and noticing that saves you from the most popular objection in the world.
summary.body:
**The principle of causality (PC).** In Feser’s precise form: *no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it*. Read it slowly, because the popular version — “everything has a cause” — is not what it says, and Feser never asserts the popular version. PC applies to the actualization of potentials. Something with no potentials to actualize falls outside its scope entirely, not by special exemption but because there is nothing there for the principle to be about.

Why believe PC? Chapter 1 offers more than one route. There is the empirical route: we never observe potentials actualizing themselves, and the general reliability of our expectations is best explained by PC’s being true. But Feser thinks the deeper support is conceptual: a merely potential F cannot do anything precisely because it is merely potential, and doing something is the prerogative of what is actual. Potential coldness cannot chill anything; only actual coldness can.

**The principle of sufficient reason (PSR).** In plain words: *everything has an explanation of why it exists and why it is as it is* — either in something else, or in itself. Two Thomistic formulations Feser quotes are that everything which is has a sufficient reason for existing, and that everything is intelligible.

Now hold PC and PSR side by side, because chapter 5 insists they are distinct principles.

- A **cause** must be distinct from its effect; nothing causes itself. A **reason** need not be distinct from what it explains; something could in principle be self-explanatory.
- PC does **not** entail that everything has a cause. PSR **does** entail that everything has a sufficient reason. Whatever has a cause has its reason in something else; if something lacks a cause, it must have its reason in itself.
- All causes are reasons, since causes make their effects intelligible. Not all reasons are causes.

**Why believe PSR?** Chapter 5 gives an inductive argument (we keep finding explanations; the world behaves as it would if PSR were true and not as it would if PSR were false), but argues that PSR is more certain than any empirical hypothesis and is best supported indirectly, by **reductio ad absurdum** — showing that denying it leads to absurdity. The central line, developed from Alexander Pruss and Robert Koons: if PSR is false, there might be no connection whatever between our perceptions and the world, and no basis even for calling such a disconnect improbable; worse, we could have no reason to think our beliefs are held *because* of good reasons rather than for no reason at all. Since that applies to any argument against PSR too, rejecting PSR is **self-undermining**.

**And brute facts.** Feser also argues that explanation terminating in an unexplained **brute fact** is not explanation at all. If a shelf stays aloft as a sheer brute fact, with no tendency of its own to do so, it cannot impart such a tendency to the book on it; the “explanation” is illusory. Same for a bottom-level law of nature: if A explains B and B explains C but A is brute, A has nothing to impart that could explain anything.
summary.takeaway: PC says no potential is actualized without something already actual to actualize it; PSR says everything has an explanation, in itself or in another — and neither amounts to “everything has a cause,” which is why “who made God?” never touches these arguments.
summary.deepDive:
**Why the difference between PC and “everything has a cause” is the single most valuable thing in this lesson.** The most repeated objection to arguments for God is: “If everything has a cause, what caused God? And if God doesn’t need a cause, why does the universe?” Feser devotes the opening of chapter 7 to it and judges it inept, for two reasons stacked on top of each other. First, no argument in the book uses the premise “everything has a cause,” so the objection attacks a **straw man**. Second — and this is the part critics usually miss — the arguments do not merely exempt God; they *explain* why the terminus could not in principle have a cause. Things need causes because they are mixtures of actuality and potentiality, or because they have parts, or because their essence is distinct from their existence, or because they are contingent. What is purely actual has no potentials to be actualized; what is absolutely simple has no parts to be assembled; what just *is* existence has no essence to be conjoined to existence; what is necessary could not have been otherwise. So “what caused God?” translates into “what actualized the potentials in that which has none?” — a question with no content.

**A worked example of PSR at work.** You come home and find an unfamiliar pair of sunglasses on the sofa. You do not conclude they popped into being; you ask around and learn a friend left them. Even when you never find the explanation — an unsolved murder — you assume there is one and often can explain why you lack it. That habit is PSR, and science shares it. A world where PSR failed would be one in which inexplicable events should be constant and the success of science would be miraculous.

**The most serious rival: brute facts.** Russell told Copleston that the universe is “just there, and that’s all.” Chapter 5 replies with the shelf and the layered laws of nature. Whether you find that convincing is one of the real questions you should keep open while reading; it is not a cheap objection, and Feser treats it seriously.

**How it feeds the arguments.** PC is step 4 of chapter 1’s fifty-step argument. PSR is the opening premise of chapter 5. And in chapter 6 Feser derives two further principles from them: the **principle of proportionate causality** (whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause somehow — formally, virtually, or eminently) and ***agere sequitur esse*** (a thing acts according to what it is).

**The usual confusion.** People treat PSR as the claim that we can always *find* the explanation. It is not an epistemological claim about our success rate; it is a claim about reality — that there is one, whether or not anyone ever discovers it.

checks.q: Feser’s principle of causality states that…
options: everything that exists has a cause
no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it
every event has a prior event in time that caused it
everything has an explanation, either in itself or in another
checks.explanation: PC concerns the actualization of potentials, not everything whatever. The last option states PSR, which is a different principle; the first is the popular caricature Feser never asserts.

checks.q: Which statement about PC and PSR is correct?
options: PSR entails that everything has a sufficient reason, while PC does not entail that everything has a cause
they are two names for the same principle
PC entails that everything has a cause, while PSR does not
a sufficient reason must always be distinct from what it explains
checks.explanation: Chapter 5 draws exactly this contrast: a cause must be distinct from its effect, but a sufficient reason need not be, so something could be self-explanatory. PC does not entail universal causation.

checks.q: The core of Feser’s reductio against denying PSR is that…
options: no scientist has ever observed a violation of PSR
PSR is true by definition of the word ‘reason’
denying PSR undermines any grounds one could have for denying PSR, since one could have no reason to think one’s beliefs track truth
denying PSR contradicts the principle of causality
checks.explanation: If PSR is false, our beliefs might be held for no reason whatsoever while falsely seeming well-grounded. That applies to the case against PSR too, so the denial is self-undermining.
